Grewal SS.lab_name: Grewal Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Grewal SS.role: Calgary biochemist who uses fruit flies to work out how nutrients and growth signals such as TOR set the size of cells, organs and the whole animal
Grewal SS.sub: Professor, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, and Senior Associate Dean (Research), Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (at Calgary since 2007) · postdoc, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (Seattle) · PhD in Cell and Developmental Biology, Oregon Health & Science University (2001) · BSc in Pharmacology, King's College London (1992)
story: Savraj Grewal is the senior author of the Atlas study SRI2026, done in fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae. A larva has one job: to eat and grow fast before it turns into an adult. Its fat body, a tissue that works like a mix of our liver and fat, senses how much food there is and sends signals that tell the rest of the body how fast to grow. The study found that TOR, the nutrient-sensing growth kinase, keeps the level of TFAM protein low in the fat body. TFAM is the protein that switches on the genes inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. TOR does this after the TFAM message has been made, not by blocking the gene itself. This TOR to TFAM link in one tissue helps decide how fast the whole larva grows. It is fly work, so it shows a mechanism in an animal, not in people.

The paper continues a line of work from the same lab. In 2022 the group showed that food changes the shape and activity of mitochondria in the fat body, and that turning down mitochondrial energy production only in this tissue made larvae grow faster, through secreted signals that boost insulin action. A 2023 paper found that macrophage-like blood cells use their mitochondria in a similar way to influence body growth.

Grewal studied pharmacology at King's College London, earned a PhD in cell and developmental biology at Oregon Health & Science University in 2001, and did postdoctoral research at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center. Grewal joined the University of Calgary in 2007. The Grewal lab uses Drosophila to study the genetic and molecular controls of cell and tissue growth, with a view to cancer and child development. Grewal is a professor in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and Senior Associate Dean (Research) at the Cumming School of Medicine, and a member of the Arnie Charbonneau Cancer Institute and the Alberta Children's Hospital Research Institute.

highlights.SRI2026: Senior author: the lab showed in fly larvae that TOR keeps the mitochondrial regulator TFAM low in the fat body, and that this link helps set whole-body growth.

Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.lab_name: Grewal Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary (Calgary, Alberta, Canada)
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.role: Fruit fly biologist in Savraj Grewal's Calgary lab who studies how growth signals and mitochondria in one tissue control how fast the whole larva grows
Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Clark H. Smith Brain Tumour Centre and Arnie Charbonneau Cancer Institute, University of Calgary (papers with Savraj Grewal, 2018–2026)
story: Shrivani Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas is the first author of the Atlas study SRI2026, from Savraj Grewal's lab at the University of Calgary. The work was done in fruit fly (Drosophila) larvae. Their fat body senses food and tells the rest of the body how fast to grow. The study found that TOR, the nutrient-sensing growth kinase, keeps the protein TFAM low in the fat body. TFAM switches on the genes inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. TOR acts on TFAM after its message is made, and this link in one tissue helps set the growth rate of the whole animal. It is a fly study and shows a mechanism, not a result in people.

The PubMed record shows a steady path in the same lab. In 2018 Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas was first author of two papers showing that the Ras/ERK growth pathway drives fly growth by boosting the cell's protein-making machinery: tRNA synthesis through the repressor Maf1, and ribosomal RNA synthesis through the factor TIF-IA. In 2022, in Cell Reports, the same team showed that lowering mitochondrial energy production only in the fat body made larvae grow faster, by reducing secreted signals that hold back insulin. A 2023 paper extended the idea to macrophage-like blood cells.
All of these papers list the University of Calgary. No separate official profile was found, so the current position is given as the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SRI2026: First author: showed in fly larvae that TOR keeps the mitochondrial regulator TFAM low in the fat body, which helps set the growth of the whole animal.

Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas S.note: No official profile found; position described from the PubMed record only.

Szwed A.lab_name: Jacinto Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University (Piscataway, New Jersey, USA)
Szwed A.role: Lead author, from Estela Jacinto's Rutgers lab, of a long Physiological Reviews article on how the two mTOR complexes are controlled and what they do in metabolism
Szwed A.sub: Jacinto Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Robert Wood Johnson Medical School, Rutgers University (at the time of the 2021 review)
story: Angelia Szwed is the first author of SZW2021, a review in Physiological Reviews written with Eugene Kim and Estela Jacinto at Rutgers. mTOR, the cell's central growth kinase, works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 reads nutrients and switches on the making of proteins, fats and nucleotides. mTORC2 responds mostly to growth factors and helps control sugar uptake, survival and the cell's skeleton. The review explains how each complex is switched on and off and what each one does to metabolism, with examples from cancer, immune cells, diabetes and obesity, brain disease and ageing.

For a student, a review of this kind is a map of the field. It is useful for seeing how the many single findings fit together, but it reports other people's experiments and does not add new data of its own.

The Jacinto lab website lists the review on a page for Szwed. PubMed shows no other papers under this name with an mTOR or Rutgers link, and no official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the review.

highlights.SZW2021: First author of a Physiological Reviews article on how mTORC1 and mTORC2 are regulated and how they control metabolism.

Szwed A.note: Only one paper found under this name; current position not confirmed.

Swarup A.lab_name: Bolger Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Georgia (Athens, Georgia, USA)
Swarup A.role: PhD candidate in Timothy Bolger's lab at the University of Georgia who studies how cancer mutations in the RNA helicase DDX3X change the cell's protein-making response to stress
Swarup A.sub: PhD candidate, BCMB program, Bolger Lab, University of Georgia · master's studies at Maastricht University and Savitribai Phule Pune University · undergraduate degree, Savitribai Phule Pune University
story: Akanksha Swarup is the first author of SWA2026, done in Timothy Bolger's lab at the University of Georgia. DDX3X is an RNA helicase, a protein that unwinds folded messenger RNA so ribosomes can read it. It is often mutated in medulloblastoma, a brain cancer of children. The team copied these cancer mutations into DED1, the yeast version of the gene. The mutant yeast kept growing in rapamycin, the drug that blocks the growth complex TORC1. After TORC1 was blocked, the mutant cells made more protein from messages with simple, unfolded starts, many of them growth messages. This hints at how mutant DDX3X might let tumour cells escape a brake set by TORC1, but it is yeast work and does not show the effect in tumours.

In 2024 Swarup and Bolger also wrote a review in Biomolecules on the role of DDX3X in medulloblastoma. The lab page lists Swarup as a PhD candidate in the Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (BCMB) program. Swarup did undergraduate studies at Savitribai Phule Pune University in India and master's studies at Maastricht University in the Netherlands and Savitribai Phule Pune University.

highlights.SWA2026: First author: modelled medulloblastoma DDX3X mutations in yeast DED1 and found rapamycin-resistant growth with more translation of simple-start growth messages after TORC1 inhibition.

Morita M.lab_name: Morita Lab, Department of Molecular Medicine and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Morita M.role: Biochemist at UT Health San Antonio who studies how mTORC1 controls protein synthesis, mRNA decay and mitochondria, and how these links go wrong in cancer and metabolic disease
Morita M.sub: Associate Professor, Department of Molecular Medicine and Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio · postdoc in cancer metabolism, McGill University (Nahum Sonenberg lab) · postdoc in medical sciences, University of Tokyo · PhD in Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of Tokyo (2008)
story: Masahiro Morita is the first author of MOR2013, a Cell Metabolism paper from Nahum Sonenberg's lab at McGill University. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, was known to switch on protein synthesis. The study showed that it also builds up and powers mitochondria, the cell's power plants, by raising the translation of messenger RNAs for mitochondrial proteins. It does this through the 4E-BP proteins, brakes on translation that mTORC1 switches off. In simple terms, when mTORC1 is active the cell makes more of the parts it needs to produce energy for growth. The work was done in cultured cells and mice.

The paper won Morita a McGill MedStar Award in 2015 as a postdoctoral fellow. A 2017 Molecular Cell paper, also with Sonenberg, followed the same thread: mTORC1 raises translation of MTFP1, a protein that drives mitochondrial fission, and when mTOR is blocked the mitochondria fuse into long networks that help cells survive.

Morita earned a BS, MS and PhD at the University of Tokyo, finishing the PhD in 2008, and did postdoctoral work there before moving to McGill. In Tokyo Morita worked with Tadashi Yamamoto on the CCR4-NOT complex, which shortens the poly(A) tails of mRNAs and so speeds their decay. Morita is now an associate professor in the Department of Molecular Medicine and the Barshop Institute at UT Health San Antonio, where the lab studies how mTOR signalling, mRNA translation and decay, and mitochondrial dynamics contribute to cancer and metabolic disease, including the role of CCR4-NOT in metabolic disorders.

highlights.MOR2013: First author: showed that mTORC1 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and activity by raising the translation of mitochondria-related mRNAs through the 4E-BPs.

Morita M.note: LAR2012 (metformin paper from the Sonenberg lab) lists a Masahiro Morita as second author without affiliation. Given the same lab and years, it is very likely the same person; curator may want to link it.

Park JM.lab_name: Do-Hyung Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Park JM.role: Autophagy researcher in Do-Hyung Kim's University of Minnesota lab who mapped how the kinase ULK1 starts autophagy, and lead author of work showing that AMPK can hold ULK1 back under energy stress
Park JM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (papers with Do-Hyung Kim, 2013–2023)
story: Ji-Man Park is the first author of PAR2023, a Nature Communications paper from Do-Hyung Kim's lab at the University of Minnesota. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane and breaks them down. The kinase ULK1 starts the process. A textbook model said that AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, switches ULK1 on when energy runs low. In cultured cells starved of glucose or with poisoned mitochondria, the team found the opposite: AMPK held ULK1 and autophagy back. AMPK also shielded the ULK1 machinery from being cut up by caspases, enzymes active in cell death, so autophagy could restart later. This challenges a common reading of how energy stress and autophagy are linked, though it comes from cell culture.

Park's PubMed record shows a long run of ULK1 work in the same lab. As first author, Park showed in 2016 that ULK1 binds and phosphorylates ATG14, a step that passes the mTORC1 signal on to the autophagy machinery, and in 2018 that ULK1 phosphorylates BECN1 (Beclin 1) on serine 30 to drive autophagy. Park also contributed to the lab's 2014 Molecular Cell paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG to slow autophagosome maturation, and co-wrote a 2023 commentary in Autophagy titled "A paradigm shift: AMPK negatively regulates ULK1 activity".
All of these papers list the University of Minnesota. No official profile page was found, so the current position could not be confirmed; the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.PAR2023: First author: found in cultured cells that AMPK restrains ULK1 and autophagy under energy stress and protects the ULK1 machinery from caspase cleavage.

Ruvinsky I.lab_name: Meyuhas Lab, Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School (Jerusalem, Israel)
Ruvinsky I.role: Biochemist from Oded Meyuhas's Jerusalem lab who made the mouse in which ribosomal protein S6 cannot be phosphorylated, showing that this mark controls cell size and blood sugar rather than the translation of TOP mRNAs
Ruvinsky I.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School, Jerusalem (papers with Oded Meyuhas, 2005–2009)
story: Igor Ruvinsky is the first author of RUV2005, a Genes & Development paper from Oded Meyuhas's lab at the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. Ribosomal protein S6 sits on the ribosome, the cell's protein-making machine, and is the best-known target of S6 kinase, which mTORC1 switches on. For years people thought that adding phosphate groups to S6 was how cells turned up the translation of 5'TOP mRNAs, the messages that code for ribosome parts. The team made knock-in mice in which all five phosphorylatable serines of S6 were changed to alanine, so S6 could never be phosphorylated. Translation of 5'TOP mRNAs did not change. Instead, cells from these mice made protein and divided faster, yet stayed smaller than normal cells, and rapamycin did not shrink them further. The mice also handled glucose poorly, a sign that their insulin-making beta cells were affected.

This was a clean genetic test of a widely held model, and it moved the role of S6 phosphorylation from translation control to cell size and metabolism. Ruvinsky and Meyuhas summed this up in a 2006 review in Trends in Biochemical Sciences, and a 2009 PLoS ONE paper from the same lab showed that the mutant mice have weak muscles, because their muscle fibres grow less and hold less ATP and phosphocreatine.

These three papers all list the Hebrew University-Hadassah Medical School. No later record could be tied to this person with confidence, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RUV2005: First author: built and analysed the S6 phosphorylation-dead knock-in mouse, showing that S6 phosphorylation sets cell size and glucose balance but is not needed for 5'TOP mRNA translation.

Ruvinsky I.note: Current position not found. PubMed also has an unrelated Ilya Ruvinsky (evolutionary biology) under 'Ruvinsky I'; only the three Meyuhas-lab papers were used.

Kim YM.lab_name: Do-Hyung Kim Lab, Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA)
Kim YM.role: mTOR researcher in Do-Hyung Kim's University of Minnesota lab who found SH3BP4 as a brake on the amino acid sensing Rag GTPases and showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG to slow autophagy
Kim YM.sub: Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota (papers with Do-Hyung Kim, 2007–2016)
story: Young-Mi Kim is the first author of KIM2012, a Molecular Cell paper from Do-Hyung Kim's lab at the University of Minnesota. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only works when it sits on the surface of the lysosome, and it is brought there by the Rag GTPases, switches that flip on when amino acids are plentiful. The study, done in human cells, found that the protein SH3BP4 binds the inactive form of the Rag complex when amino acids are scarce and keeps it from switching on. As a result mTORC1 stays away from the lysosome, its activity and cell growth drop, and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, goes up.

Kim followed this with a short 2012 review on SH3BP4 and other Rag binders in Molecules and Cells, and was first author of the lab's 2014 Molecular Cell paper showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates UVRAG, a protein that helps autophagosomes and endosomes mature. Phosphorylation of UVRAG slows that maturation, so mTORC1 brakes autophagy at a late step as well as at the start. Earlier papers in the same lab, from 2007 and 2009, include the discovery of PRR5 as a part of mTORC2 and the finding that mTOR phosphorylates the ULK-ATG13-FIP200 complex that starts autophagy.

These papers all list the University of Minnesota. Because this is a common name, only papers shared with Do-Hyung Kim at Minnesota were counted. No official profile was found, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KIM2012: First author: identified SH3BP4 as a protein that binds inactive Rag GTPases under amino acid shortage and keeps mTORC1 off.

Kim YM.note: Common name; identity tied through Do-Hyung Kim and University of Minnesota only. Current position not confirmed.

Meng D.lab_name: Bandyopadhyay Lab, Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Meng D.role: Cancer researcher at UCSF who led the preclinical test of RMC-6272, a drug that blocks mTORC1 much more strongly than mTORC2, in drug-resistant breast cancer
Meng D.sub: Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (at the time of the 2023 study, with Sourav Bandyopadhyay)
story: Delong Meng is the first author of MEN2023, an Oncogene paper from Sourav Bandyopadhyay's group at UCSF, written with colleagues at Revolution Medicines, the company that makes the drug. mTOR works in two complexes. mTORC1 drives growth, and in many breast cancers it stays switched on because of mutations in PIK3CA or PTEN. Older drugs either block mTORC1 only partly, like rapamycin, which misses the target 4E-BP1, or block both complexes, which causes side effects such as high blood sugar. RMC-6272 is a bi-steric inhibitor: one molecule that grips mTOR at two sites at once. It is more than 25 times more selective for mTORC1 than for mTORC2 and shuts mTORC1 down completely, including its control of 4E-BP1.

In the study the drug killed ER-positive breast cancer cell lines, especially those with PIK3CA or PTEN mutations, and still worked in models that had become resistant to hormone therapy and to CDK4/6 inhibitors. The tests used cell lines and patient tumours grown in mice (PDX models), so they are preclinical. The paper laid groundwork for the related drug RMC-5552, which has gone into clinical trials.

PubMed shows no other paper that can be tied to this name with the same co-authors, and no official profile was found, so the current position could not be confirmed. The affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MEN2023: First author: showed that the mTORC1-selective bi-steric inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes hormone- and CDK4/6-inhibitor resistance in breast cancer cell lines and PDX models.

Meng D.note: Only one paper found; current position not confirmed.

Suzuki C.lab_name: Wagner Lab, Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Suzuki C.role: Structural biologist from Gerhard Wagner's Harvard lab who showed how the tumour suppressor PDCD4 grabs the helicase eIF4A to block the start of protein synthesis
Suzuki C.sub: Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School (papers with Gerhard Wagner, 2008–2009)
story: Chikako Suzuki is the first author of SUZ2008, a PNAS paper from Gerhard Wagner's lab at Harvard Medical School. To start making a protein, the cell must unwind the front end of a messenger RNA. The helicase eIF4A does the unwinding, helped by the scaffold protein eIF4G. PDCD4 is a tumour suppressor that blocks this step, and mTORC1 signalling, through S6 kinase, marks PDCD4 for destruction so that translation can go ahead.

Using x-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy and binding measurements on purified proteins, the team showed that both MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind the front part of eIF4A. In doing so PDCD4 competes with eIF4G and with RNA for the same helicase. This explains in physical terms how PDCD4 slows the start of translation. The work is on purified proteins, so it shows a mechanism, not an effect in cells or animals.

Suzuki is also a co-author of a 2009 Cell paper from the same lab, with Nahum Sonenberg's group, that mapped how eIF4A, eIF4G and eIF4H fit together into a working helicase complex. Because this is a common name, only papers shared with Wagner were counted. No later record could be tied to this person, so the current position is not known and the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SUZ2008: First author: solved how both MA3 domains of PDCD4 bind eIF4A and compete with eIF4G and RNA, explaining how PDCD4 blocks translation initiation.

Suzuki C.note: Common name; current position not found. The 2008 paper also appears in the University of Basel repository (edoc), which may reflect a co-author's affiliation rather than Suzuki's.

Ramanathan C.lab_name: College of Health Sciences, University of Memphis (Memphis, Tennessee, USA)
Ramanathan C.role: Circadian biologist at the University of Memphis who showed that mTOR signalling sets the speed and strength of the body's daily clocks
Ramanathan C.sub: Research Associate Professor, College of Health Sciences, University of Memphis · postdoc in circadian functional genomics, University of Memphis · postdoc on the neural basis of day-active behaviour, Michigan State University · PhD, Madurai Kamaraj University (2002)
story: Chidambaram (Chida) Ramanathan is the first author of RAM2018, a PLoS Genetics paper from Andrew Liu's group at the University of Memphis. Almost every cell runs a circadian clock, a set of genes that switch each other on and off over about 24 hours. A master clock in the brain, the SCN, keeps the clocks in organs such as the liver in step. The study started from the observation that mTOR activity itself rises and falls over the day, and asked whether mTOR also feeds back on the clock.

It does. Blocking mTOR made the clock run slower, with a longer period, and weaker, with a flatter rhythm. Turning mTOR up did the reverse. The team saw this in cultured cells, in slices of SCN and liver taken from mice, and in living mice with only one working copy of the mTOR gene, whose daily activity cycle ran longer. This links the cell's main nutrient and growth sensor to the timing of daily rhythms, though the evidence comes from cells and mice.

Ramanathan earned a PhD at Madurai Kamaraj University in India in 2002, then worked as a postdoc at Michigan State University on the brain basis of being active by day, and at the University of Memphis on circadian functional genomics. Ramanathan is now a research associate professor in the College of Health Sciences at the University of Memphis, studying how circadian clocks and their output signals interact with cell metabolism, oxidative stress and ageing.

highlights.RAM2018: First author: showed in cells, mouse tissue slices and mTOR heterozygous mice that mTOR activity sets the period and amplitude of central and peripheral circadian clocks.

Pacold ME.lab_name: Pacold Lab, Department of Radiation Oncology and Laura and Isaac Perlmutter Cancer Center, NYU Langone Health (New York, New York, USA)
Pacold ME.role: Radiation oncologist and chemical biologist at NYU Langone who studies the metabolism of brain tumours, and a co-author of the Sabatini lab's structure of the leucine sensor Sestrin2
Pacold ME.sub: Assistant Professor of Radiation Oncology, NYU Langone Health · postdoc, David Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute and MIT, with Department of Radiation Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (2010s) · earlier structural work, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge (Roger Williams group, 2001)
story: Michael Pacold is a co-author of SAX2015, a Science paper from David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute and MIT. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only switches on when amino acids are present, and leucine is one of the most important. Sestrin2 is the protein that senses leucine for mTORC1. The team solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine. It shows a single pocket for leucine, closed by a lid-like loop. When the pocket was mutated so that it held leucine less tightly, cells needed more leucine before mTORC1 switched on. This tied a physical shape to a signalling job.

Pacold's training mixed structural biology and medicine. In 2001 Pacold was a co-author, with Roger Williams's group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, of the crystal structure of the PX domain of p40phox bound to a lipid. As a postdoc in the Sabatini lab, while also linked to the Department of Radiation Oncology at Dana-Farber, Pacold was first author of a 2016 Nature Chemical Biology paper describing a small-molecule inhibitor of PHGDH, the first enzyme in the pathway that makes serine from glucose, and showing how serine synthesis guides the use of one-carbon units for building DNA.

Pacold now leads a lab at NYU Langone Health as Assistant Professor of Radiation Oncology. The lab uses chemical biology, enzymology, structural biology and mass spectrometry to find the metabolic adaptations that let tumour cells survive in unusual settings, especially in the brain, and to design inhibitors against them.

highlights.SAX2015: Co-author on the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, which revealed the pocket that makes it a leucine sensor for mTORC1.

Pacold ME.note: KAN2013 also lists a Pacold ME without affiliation; very likely the same person (Sabatini lab, same years). PhD/MD details could not be confirmed from an official page (web search budget ran out).

Brignole EJ.lab_name: Department of Biology and MIT.nano, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Brignole EJ.role: Electron microscopy specialist at MIT whose cryo-EM work helped solve the structures of GATOR1, GATOR2 and Raptor docked on the Rag GTPases for the Sabatini lab
Brignole EJ.sub: Department of Biology and MIT.nano, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (2018–2022 Atlas papers) · long-standing structural work with Catherine Drennan's group at MIT
story: Edward Brignole is a co-author of three structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, all made with cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In cryo-EM, purified proteins are frozen in a thin layer of ice and photographed thousands of times with an electron beam, and the images are combined into a 3D model. The method needs careful sample preparation and microscope work, which is where an EM specialist comes in.

The three papers solve key parts of how mTORC1 senses amino acids. SHE2018 gives the structure of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rag GTPases off, alone and bound to the Rags, and shows how it does so. ROG2019 shows how Raptor, part of mTORC1, docks onto the Rag-Ragulator complex on the lysosome: one part of Raptor reads the state of RagA and a separate claw reads RagC, and only the right combination lets mTORC1 land. VAL2022 gives the structure of human GATOR2, a large cage-like complex built on an octagonal frame, and maps where the sensors Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 attach. How GATOR2 holds back GATOR1 is still not fully settled.

Brignole's PubMed record shows a long collaboration with Catherine Drennan's group at MIT, with fifteen joint papers up to 2023. The Atlas papers list the MIT Department of Biology and MIT.nano, the institute's shared imaging facility. No official profile page was found, so the exact current title is not given here.

highlights.VAL2022: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure of human GATOR2, a large cage that carries the binding sites for Sestrin2 and CASTOR1.
highlights.ROG2019: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure showing how Raptor docks on Rag-Ragulator to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.SHE2018: Co-author on the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 alone and bound to the Rag GTPases.

sources: PubMed search Brignole EJ[Author] AND Drennan CL[Author] (15 records, 2012-2023)
Brignole EJ.note: Current title not confirmed (no official page found; web search budget ran out).

Knockenhauer KE.role: Structural biologist trained in Thomas Schwartz's MIT lab who helped solve the amino acid sensor structures of Sestrin2 and CASTOR1, and who later moved to drug discovery at Accent Therapeutics
Knockenhauer KE.sub: Accent Therapeutics, Lexington, Massachusetts (papers 2023–2025) · Thomas Schwartz lab, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (papers 2015–2020)
story: Kevin Knockenhauer is a co-author of two structural papers in the Atlas from David Sabatini's lab, both made in collaboration with Thomas Schwartz's crystallography lab at MIT. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on only when amino acids are present, and dedicated sensor proteins tell it which amino acids are there. SAX2015 solved the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine and showed the pocket, closed by a lid-like loop, that makes it a leucine sensor. SAX2016 did the same for CASTOR1 and arginine, and showed how arginine binding makes CASTOR1 let go of GATOR2, which releases the brake on mTORC1. Both are structures of purified proteins, backed by tests in cells.

Knockenhauer's PubMed record lists twelve papers with Schwartz between 2015 and 2020; the Schwartz lab works mainly on the structure of the machinery that moves molecules across the nuclear envelope, the double membrane around the nucleus. From 2023 to 2025 the papers list Accent Therapeutics in Lexington, Massachusetts, a drug discovery company. One 2023 paper, for example, describes assays and a crystal structure for the RNA helicase DHX9 as a cancer drug target. The current position is taken from these papers; no official profile was found.

highlights.SAX2016: Co-author on the structure of CASTOR1 bound to arginine, which showed how arginine releases CASTOR1 from GATOR2.
highlights.SAX2015: Co-author on the crystal structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine, which revealed its leucine-binding pocket.

sources: PubMed search Knockenhauer KE[Author] AND Schwartz TU[Author] (12 records)
PubMed search Knockenhauer KE[Author] AND Accent[Affiliation] (5 records, 2023-2025)
Knockenhauer KE.note: Whether the MIT period was PhD or postdoc could not be confirmed. Current employer inferred from 2023-2025 papers.

Schwartz TU.lab_name: Schwartz Lab, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Schwartz TU.role: MIT structural biologist who studies how molecules pass across the nuclear envelope, and whose crystallography lab helped solve the leucine and arginine sensor structures upstream of mTORC1
Schwartz TU.sub: Boris Magasanik Professor in Biology, Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology · PhD, Free University of Berlin (2000)
story: Thomas Schwartz is a co-author of two Atlas papers, made with David Sabatini's lab, on how mTORC1 senses amino acids. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on only when amino acids are present, and sensor proteins report on single amino acids. SAX2015 gives the crystal structure of Sestrin2 holding leucine and shows a pocket closed by a lid-like loop. SAX2016 gives the structure of CASTOR1 holding arginine and shows how arginine binding makes CASTOR1 release GATOR2, lifting a brake on mTORC1. These are structures of purified proteins, backed by tests in cells. They turned the idea of an amino acid sensor into a picture at the level of atoms.

Schwartz's own research is on communication across biological membranes. The lab uses structural, biochemical and genetic tools to study how signals and molecules move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm through the nuclear envelope, and how the nuclear pore and its transport machinery are built. Schwartz earned a PhD at the Free University of Berlin in 2000 and is now the Boris Magasanik Professor in Biology at MIT.

highlights.SAX2016: Co-author: the Schwartz crystallography lab helped solve the structure of CASTOR1 bound to arginine.
highlights.SAX2015: Co-author: the Schwartz crystallography lab helped solve the structure of Sestrin2 bound to leucine.

Nicastro R.lab_name: De Virgilio Lab, Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
Nicastro R.role: Cell biologist at the University of Fribourg who studies TORC1 signalling in yeast and mammals, and first author of the discovery that malonyl-CoA is a natural mTORC1 inhibitor
Nicastro R.sub: Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (papers 2016–2026, many with Claudio De Virgilio) · earlier papers with an affiliation in Milan, Italy (2014–2015)
story: Raffaele Nicastro is the first author of NIC2023, a Nature Cell Biology paper by groups at the University of Fribourg and Constantinos Demetriades's lab. mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that uses ATP to tag other proteins. The study found that malonyl-CoA, a small molecule made on the way to building fatty acids, fits directly into the mTOR catalytic pocket and competes with ATP. It works like a natural version of the ATP-competitive mTOR drugs. When the fat-making enzyme fatty acid synthase is turned down, malonyl-CoA builds up and dampens mTORC1. This ties the cell's capacity to make fat to its overall growth output. The effect was seen in yeast and mammalian cells, which is why the paper calls it conserved.

Nicastro's PubMed record shows many papers from the University of Fribourg between 2016 and 2026 many of them with Claudio De Virgilio, whose group studies how TORC1 is controlled in yeast. Papers from 2014 and 2015 list an affiliation in Milan, Italy. No official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.NIC2023: First author: showed that malonyl-CoA binds the mTOR catalytic pocket and acts as a conserved, ATP-competitive inhibitor of mTORC1.

Vellai T.lab_name: Department of Genetics, Eötvös Loránd University (Budapest, Hungary)
Vellai T.role: Hungarian geneticist who showed in 2003 that silencing the TOR gene roughly doubles the lifespan of the worm C. elegans, and who studies autophagy and ageing in worms at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest
Vellai T.sub: Department of Genetics, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, and HUN-REN-ELTE Genetics Research Group · Department of Biology, University of Fribourg (at the time of the 2003 study, with Fritz Müller)
story: Tibor Vellai is the first author of VEL2003, a short Nature paper from Fritz Müller's group at the University of Fribourg in Switzerland. The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has a single TOR gene. When the team silenced it, the worms lived about twice as long. This was one of the first signs that turning TOR down can lengthen life in an animal. Because worms and mammals are separated by a very long stretch of evolution, the result suggested that the link between TOR and ageing is ancient. It is a worm study and does not by itself show anything about people.

Vellai went on to lead a genetics group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) in Budapest, Hungary. PubMed lists close to a hundred papers with an ELTE or Budapest affiliation under this name, many on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and its role in ageing in C. elegans. A 2025 paper, for example, describes new single-copy reporter genes that track autophagy in the worm and shows that starvation switches autophagy on only after a delay.
Recent papers list the Department of Genetics at ELTE and the HUN-REN-ELTE Genetics Research Group. No official profile page was opened, so the exact title is not given here.

highlights.VEL2003: First author: showed that silencing the single TOR gene of C. elegans roughly doubles worm lifespan.

Song H.lab_name: Oh Lab, Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (Gwangju, South Korea)
Song H.role: Researcher in Chang-Myung Oh's lab at GIST who tested urolithin A, a gut-microbe product, in mice with a stiff-heart form of heart failure
Song H.sub: Department of Biomedical Science and Engineering, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (papers with Chang-Myung Oh)
story: Hangyul Song is the first author of SONH2026, a study in Experimental and Molecular Medicine from Chang-Myung Oh's lab at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) in South Korea. It deals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): the heart still pumps out a normal share of its blood with each beat, but the muscle is stiff and thick and fills poorly. HFpEF is common in older people with obesity and diabetes and has few good treatments.

Urolithin A is made by gut bacteria from compounds in foods such as pomegranates and walnuts. In mice with HFpEF it eased heart stiffness, thickening and scarring. In heart cells it switched on AMPK, the energy sensor, and lowered mTOR activity. That restored mitophagy, the clearing of damaged mitochondria. Urolithin A also changed the gut microbiome and lowered ceramides, fatty molecules that harm heart cells. The results come from mice and cell models, not from patients.
PubMed lists several papers shared by Song and Oh. No separate profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SONH2026: First author: showed in HFpEF mice that urolithin A restores mitophagy through AMPK activation and mTOR inhibition and lowers ceramides through the gut microbiome.

story: Chang-Myung Oh is the senior author of SONH2026, with Hangyul Song as first author. The study looks at heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), in which the heart pumps a normal share of blood per beat but its muscle is stiff and fills poorly. Urolithin A, a compound that gut bacteria make from foods such as pomegranates, improved heart function and structure in HFpEF mice. It activated AMPK, the cell's energy sensor, turned down mTOR, and so restored mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria. It also lowered blood ceramides, fatty molecules linked to heart damage, through changes in the gut microbiome. These findings come from mice and cell models.

PubMed lists more than seventy papers under this name with a GIST affiliation. No official profile page could be opened, so the title and training are not given here, and the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

Jackson LN.lab_name: Mockett Lab, Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (Mobile, Alabama, USA)
Jackson LN.role: Researcher in Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama who showed that rapamycin's effect on fruit fly lifespan swings from harmful to helpful depending on the food
Jackson LN.sub: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of South Alabama (at the time of the 2026 study)
story: Lauren Jackson is the first author of JAC2026, a GeroScience paper from Robin Mockett's lab at the University of South Alabama. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, is often described as a drug that lengthens life in many animals. This fruit fly (Drosophila) study tested that claim carefully across five fly strains, both sexes and two kinds of food.

The answer depended on the diet. On a cornmeal and torula yeast food, rapamycin shortened life in 19 of 26 experiments. On a richer brewer's yeast food it helped in 8 experiments, made no difference in 14, and never caused clear harm. Changes in median lifespan ranged from a 51 percent loss to a 5 percent gain and varied with sex and strain. Rapamycin was also toxic to developing flies at higher doses. The lesson for a reader is that a lifespan result in one lab, on one food, may not carry over to other conditions. It is a fly study, so it says nothing direct about people.
PubMed shows only this paper under this name with Mockett, and no official profile was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.JAC2026: First author: showed across five fly strains that rapamycin's effect on lifespan depends on diet, from clearly harmful to modestly helpful.

Heim MH.lab_name: Department of Biomedicine, University of Basel, and Clarunis (Basel, Switzerland)
Heim MH.role: Basel hepatologist who studies how the liver responds to viral infection and how liver cancer develops, and a co-author of the study linking mTORC2 to fat synthesis in liver tumours
Heim MH.sub: Department of Biomedicine, University of Basel, and Clarunis, Basel (recent papers) · Department of Biomedicine, University Hospital Basel (at the time of the 2017 study)
story: Markus Heim is a co-author of GUR2017, a Cancer Cell paper led by Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum in Basel. The team used a mouse model in which overactive mTOR signalling in the liver causes fatty liver that later turns into liver cancer. They found that mTORC2, the second mTOR complex, drives the cell's own production of fatty acids and of sphingolipids, a class of membrane fats. Blocking the making of fatty acids or sphingolipids prevented tumours in these mice. In tissue from people with liver cancer, higher lipid synthesis went along with higher mTORC2 activity, which links the mouse result to human tumours, though only as an association.

Heim's contribution came from the clinical and liver biology side in Basel. PubMed lists close to sixty papers under this name with a Basel affiliation on interferon or hepatitis C, the line of work on how the liver's antiviral interferon system responds to hepatitis viruses, and a similar number on hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common liver cancer. Recent papers, up to 2026, also list Clarunis, a university centre for digestive and liver diseases in Basel.
No official profile page could be opened, so title and training are not given here. Other Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation in PubMed and were not counted.

highlights.GUR2017: Co-author on the Basel study showing that mTORC2 drives fatty acid and sphingolipid synthesis to promote liver cancer in mice, with a matching pattern in human tumours.

Allison DB.lab_name: Department of Biostatistics, University of Alabama at Birmingham (Birmingham, Alabama, USA)
Allison DB.role: Biostatistician and obesity researcher, long at the University of Alabama at Birmingham and later dean of public health at Indiana University, known for work on nutrition, obesity and research rigour
Allison DB.sub: Dean, Indiana University School of Public Health-Bloomington (appointed 2017) · Distinguished Professor, Quetelet Endowed Professor and Director of the NIH Nutrition Obesity Research Center, University of Alabama at Birmingham · fellowship, Columbia University and St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center (1994) · postdoc, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (1991) · PhD, Hofstra University (1990)
story: David Allison is a co-author of MAT2017, a Nature Communications paper that brought together the two long-running studies of caloric restriction in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging and one at the University of Wisconsin. The two studies had seemed to disagree: Wisconsin reported longer survival with fewer calories, the NIA study did not. Looking at both side by side, the authors found that calorie-restricted monkeys were healthier in both studies. Whether they also lived longer depended on how each study was designed, including the age at which restriction started and what the control monkeys ate. Monkeys are close relatives of humans, so these studies are among the best animal evidence on eating less and ageing. Caloric restriction is one of the conditions in which mTOR activity falls, which is why it appears in this Atlas.

Allison's part in such work is mainly statistical. After a PhD at Hofstra University in 1990, with a thesis on types of obese persons, he did postdoctoral work at Johns Hopkins and a fellowship at Columbia University and St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center. At the University of Alabama at Birmingham he was a Distinguished Professor, Quetelet Endowed Professor and Director of the NIH-funded Nutrition Obesity Research Center. His research covers obesity and nutrition, biostatistics, quantitative genetics and clinical trials, and the rigour and reproducibility of research; he helped organise a 2017 National Academy of Sciences colloquium on reproducibility.

In 2017 Allison was appointed dean of the Indiana University School of Public Health-Bloomington. The current position after that could not be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MAT2017: Co-author of the joint analysis of the NIA and Wisconsin monkey studies, which found health benefits of caloric restriction in both and survival effects that depended on study design.

Ito Y.lab_name: Department of Breast Medical Oncology, Cancer Institute Hospital, Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research (Tokyo, Japan)
Ito Y.role: Breast medical oncologist at the Cancer Institute Hospital in Tokyo and a co-investigator of BOLERO-2, the trial that brought the mTOR inhibitor everolimus into breast cancer treatment
Ito Y.sub: Department of Breast Medical Oncology, Cancer Institute Hospital of the Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research, Tokyo (at the time of BOLERO-2)
story: Yoshinori Ito is a co-author of the two BOLERO-2 papers in the Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had grown despite an aromatase inhibitor. In such tumours, resistance to hormone therapy is linked to overactive mTOR signalling. All women received the hormone drug exemestane, and half also received everolimus, an mTORC1 inhibitor related to rapamycin.

BAS2012, in the New England Journal of Medicine, reported the main result: adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again, from 4.1 to 10.6 months by central review, which led to approval of the combination. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis). PIC2014, in Annals of Oncology, gave the final overall survival: 31.0 months with everolimus and 26.6 months with placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant. Together the two papers show both what mTOR blockade can do in a common cancer and its limits.

In large international trials like this, many hospitals enrol patients, and their investigators appear as co-authors. PubMed lists about fifty breast cancer papers under this name from the Department of Breast Medical Oncology of the Cancer Institute Hospital. No official profile was opened, so the current title is not given here.

highlights.BAS2012: Co-author (trial investigator) of the BOLERO-2 primary report: everolimus plus exemestane more than doubled progression-free survival.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author (trial investigator) of the final BOLERO-2 overall survival report, which found no significant survival gain.
